objectives: Recognize when stream processing beats batch.

slides.title: Kafka, the durable distributed log
slides.body:
**Apache Kafka** was created at **LinkedIn** around 2010–2011 by **Jay Kreps**, **Neha Narkhede**, and **Jun Rao**. The engineers needed a system to reliably move activity stream data (page views, clicks, logs) at LinkedIn's scale — existing message queues (RabbitMQ, ActiveMQ) lacked the durability and throughput required. Kafka was open-sourced through the **Apache Software Foundation** in 2011 and graduated as a top-level Apache project in 2012. Kreps, Narkhede, and Rao later co-founded **Confluent** (2014) to build a commercial platform around Kafka.

The intellectual foundation is the **log abstraction**. Jay Kreps described it in his seminal 2013 engineering blog post *"The Log: What every software engineer should know about real-time data's unifying abstraction"*: a log is a totally ordered, append-only sequence of records with positions (offsets). Every distributed system — databases, consensus protocols, stream processors — fundamentally relies on a log to order events. Kafka externalises this internal structure as a first-class service.

**Core architecture**:
- **Topic**: a named, partitioned, append-only log. Data is split across **partitions** for parallelism. Each message within a partition has a monotonically increasing **offset**.
- **Broker**: a Kafka server that stores and serves partitions. A cluster has multiple brokers; each partition is replicated across N brokers (typically 3) for durability.
- **Producer**: writes records to a topic, optionally specifying a partition key (which determines partition assignment via consistent hashing).
- **Consumer**: reads records from one or more partitions, tracking its own **offset** per partition.
- **Consumer group**: a set of consumers sharing work. Each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer in the group, enabling horizontal parallelism. Multiple independent consumer groups can each consume the same topic at their own offsets — Kafka is a multi-consumer, fan-out system.

**Why this design wins**:
- **Durability**: each message replicated to N brokers; survives broker failure.
- **Replayability**: consumers track their own offset; can restart from any point or reprocess historical data.
- **Throughput**: append-only writes + sequential disk reads (zero-copy via sendfile) sustain millions of messages/sec per broker.
- **Decoupling**: producers and consumers evolve independently; adding a consumer requires no producer changes.

slides.title: Worked example: Kafka lag monitoring at scale
slides.body:
Production Kafka: monitor consumer lag (offset gap between latest message + consumer's processed offset) per consumer group + partition. Sustained lag growth = consumer can't keep up. **Burrow** (open-sourced by **LinkedIn**) is the standard lag-monitoring tool. Auto-scaling consumers on lag growth = standard pattern. Spikes are normal; sustained growth is an action item.

**KRaft and the ZooKeeper transition**: historically Kafka relied on **Apache ZooKeeper** (a distributed coordination service) to store cluster metadata, elect controllers, and manage partition leadership. ZooKeeper was a significant operational dependency. **KIP-500** (Kafka Improvement Proposal 500) proposed replacing ZooKeeper with a built-in Raft-based metadata quorum called **KRaft** (Kafka Raft). KRaft reached production-ready status in **Kafka 3.3** (2022) and became the default in **Kafka 3.7** (2024). KRaft reduces operational complexity, improves scalability, and allows Kafka to manage millions of partitions.

**Log compaction**: by default Kafka retains messages for a configured time or size window and then deletes old segments. Log compaction is an alternative retention policy: Kafka retains the most recent value for each message key and discards older values. This turns a Kafka topic into a compacted changelog — useful for materialised views, configuration stores, and change data capture (CDC). A new consumer can replay the compacted log to reconstruct the latest state without needing a snapshot.

question.question: Derive consumer-lag accumulation rate
question.goal: Producer rate $P$ msg/s. Consumer rate $C$ msg/s. If $C < P$, lag grows at rate?

steps.prompt: Per second: $P$ new messages arrive; consumer processes $C$. Net new lag: $P - C$.
steps.reveal: Lag grows at $P - C$ msg/s. If $C \geq P$: lag flat (steady state) or shrinking.

question.finalResult: $$\boxed{\text{Lag growth rate} = P - C}$$ Sustained $C < P$ → unbounded lag → eventually consumer is 'behind' by hours. Mitigations: scale consumer count, optimize consumer code, partition more aggressively (more consumers parallel). Alerting on lag growth catches the issue before it's a customer-facing problem.

slides.title: At-least-once vs exactly-once, Kafka Streams, and the streaming ecosystem
slides.body:
**Delivery semantics** are a fundamental distributed-systems trade-off:

- **At-most-once**: messages may be lost but never duplicated. Achieved by committing the offset before processing; if the consumer crashes post-commit but pre-processing, the message is skipped.
- **At-least-once**: every message is processed at least once; duplicates are possible. Achieved by committing the offset after processing; if the consumer crashes post-processing but pre-commit, the message is replayed. This is Kafka's default and the most common production choice.
- **Exactly-once**: every message is processed exactly once. Kafka 0.11 (2017) introduced **idempotent producers** (each message carries a sequence number; the broker deduplicates retries) and **transactional APIs** (atomically write to multiple partitions and commit offsets). Together these enable exactly-once semantics (EOS) for Kafka-to-Kafka pipelines. End-to-end exactly-once (Kafka to a downstream database) requires the downstream to participate in the transaction.

In practice most teams implement **idempotent consumers** on top of at-least-once: design the consumer so that processing a duplicate message produces the same result as processing it once (upsert by ID, conditional writes). This is far cheaper to operate than transactional EOS and handles the same failure modes.

**Kafka Streams** (introduced in Kafka 0.10, 2016) is a client library for building stream-processing applications directly on top of Kafka — no separate cluster (unlike Apache Flink or Apache Spark Streaming). It provides a DSL for map, filter, join, aggregate, windowed aggregations, and table-topic joins (KTables). State stores are backed by local RocksDB instances with Kafka changelog topics for durability.

**Event sourcing and change data capture (CDC)**:
- **Event sourcing**: store application state as an immutable sequence of events rather than current state. Kafka is the natural event log. Re-applying the event log rebuilds any point-in-time state.
- **CDC**: capture every row-level change in a relational database (inserts, updates, deletes) and publish them as Kafka messages. Tools: **Debezium** (Red Hat, open source), which reads database write-ahead logs (Postgres WAL, MySQL binlog, SQL Server CDC). CDC enables real-time data pipelines without polling the source database.

**Competing and complementary systems**:
- **Apache Pulsar** (Yahoo, 2016; Apache 2018): separates storage (Apache BookKeeper) from serving, enabling near-infinite retention and multi-tenancy. Claims better geo-replication than Kafka.
- **Amazon Kinesis** (AWS, 2013): managed Kafka-like streaming service. Simpler operational model (no cluster to run) but lower throughput ceiling and less flexible consumer model than Kafka.
- **Confluent Platform**: Confluent's commercial distribution adds the **Schema Registry** (enforces Avro/JSON/Protobuf schemas on topics), **ksqlDB** (SQL interface for stream processing), and managed cloud Kafka.

Kafka's combination of durability, throughput, replay, and multi-consumer fan-out makes it the default choice for high-volume event streaming as of 2025.

question.question: Consumer offsets in Kafka are:
options: Stored on the broker, managed by Kafka.
Tracked by each consumer group; allows different consumers to read at different positions in the same log.
question.explanation: Consumer offset = the position in a partition the consumer has read up to. Each consumer group tracks its own offsets, stored on a special internal Kafka topic. Two consumer groups can read the same partition at completely different offsets — that's what makes Kafka multi-consumer. The producer doesn't know or care about consumer offsets.

hints: What does 'offset' mean in the context of an append-only log?
Multiple consumer groups can read the same partition — what does that imply about offset ownership?
slides.workedSolution: Each consumer group maintains its own offsets per partition — the position up to which the group has acknowledged consumption. Offsets are stored in a special internal Kafka topic (__consumer_offsets). Two consumer groups consuming the same partition can be at completely different positions in the log — that's how Kafka enables multi-consumer fan-out without producers caring about it.

question.question: Stream or batch?
question.prompt: Your team is choosing between a Kafka-based streaming pipeline and a batch dbt pipeline for the same fraud-detection use case. Walk through the decision: when does the latency win of streaming actually matter, and when is batch simpler + sufficient?

question.question: Kafka topic with 12 partitions, each broker can sustain 100MB/s/partition. Max sustained throughput (MB/s)?

question.prompt: Explain in two or three sentences why most production teams use at-least-once + idempotent consumers, even though exactly-once is available.
question.rubric: Mentions that at-least-once + idempotency on the consumer side is cheaper to operate than transactional exactly-once across heterogeneous systems; idempotent consumers are testable + composable + handle the failure modes (consumer restart, broker failover) gracefully.
